title: Anagram
directAnswer: If the length is odd, the answer is −1 (you can't split into two equal halves). Otherwise split the string into halves a and b, count the character frequencies of each, and the minimum number of changes equals the sum of the positive surpluses of a over b — i.e. for every letter, how many more times it appears in a than in b. That equals (sum of absolute frequency differences) / 2. O(n) time, O(1) space (26 counters).

remember.formula:
n = len(s)
if n is odd: return -1
a, b = s[:n/2], s[n/2:]
count = freq(a) - freq(b)   # per character
return sum(c for c in count if c > 0)   # == sum(|c|)/2
rules: Odd length → immediately **−1**; halves of unequal size can never be anagrams.
You only need to change characters in **one** half — count surplus letters in `a`, not both directions.
Sum of **positive** differences equals `sum(|diff|)/2` — each surplus in `a` pairs with a deficit in `b`.
26 fixed counters means **O(1) space**, not O(n) — say this out loud.
Changing a character is one operation; you never delete or insert, only replace.
whenToUse: Two equal-length strings (or two halves) and you need edits to make them anagrams
The cost is defined per-character-replacement, not per-deletion
Order doesn't matter — only multiset of characters
Lowercase-only alphabet so a fixed 26-slot array works
antiSignals: Deletions allowed from both strings → Making Anagrams (sum of all |diffs|, not /2)
You must check equality, not count edits → just compare sorted strings or frequency maps
Unicode / huge alphabet → use a hash map, not a 26-array
Substrings / sliding window of anagrams → that's a different (window) pattern
remember.takeaway: Replacing characters in one half to match the other costs exactly the number of surplus letters in that half. Because every surplus in `a` is mirrored by a deficit in `b`, summing positive differences (or `sum(|diff|)/2`) gives the answer in one frequency pass.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reduce 'make these anagrams' to a pure frequency-count problem, and whether you correctly count edits as surplus-in-one-half rather than double-counting both halves.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Summing the absolute differences without dividing by two (that's the Making Anagrams answer, where both strings can be edited), or forgetting the odd-length → −1 guard.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State that one replacement fixes one surplus-and-deficit pair simultaneously, so the answer is the surplus count, equivalently sum(|diff|)/2. Mention the fixed 26-array gives O(1) space.

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, split it into two halves: the first half `a` and the second half `b`. Determine the **minimum number of character changes** needed to make `b` an anagram of `a` (changing a character means replacing it with any other character).

If the length of `s` is **odd**, the two halves cannot have equal length, so it is impossible — return `-1`.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters only
A 'change' replaces one character with any other (no insert/delete)
understanding: Anagram means same letters, same counts, any order. Splitting `s` in half gives two windows of equal size (when the length is even). We may rewrite letters in the second half; the cheapest way to make it an anagram of the first is to count, per letter, how many extra copies the first half has that the second lacks — each such surplus is one forced replacement.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens on odd length?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return −1. Two halves of different sizes can't be anagrams no matter how many changes you make.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I edit both halves?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The problem only asks to change characters in one half to match the other. Editing both is the related 'Making Anagrams' problem.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a change a replacement or a delete?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A replacement — swap a character for any other. Lengths stay equal, so deletes aren't involved.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What alphabet?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Lowercase a–z, so 26 integer counters suffice — O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: a = "aaa", b = "bbb". The first half has 3 surplus 'a's that the second half lacks, so all 3 'b's must become 'a's. 3 changes.
a = "xaxb" (x:2, a:1, b:1), b = "bbxx" (b:2, x:2). Surplus of a over b: a:+1 (b:−1 cancels). Only one change needed.
Odd length 3 — cannot split into two equal halves.

diagrams.title: Split, count, sum the surplus
diagrams.caption: Odd length short-circuits to −1; otherwise the answer is the positive frequency difference between the halves.

approaches.name: Sort Each Half and Compare Letter Counts (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention to show you understand 'anagram = same multiset', then note sorting is overkill versus counting.
hints: Two strings are anagrams iff their sorted forms are identical. How could sorting help you measure the gap?
Sort both halves. Walk them together; every position where they disagree hints at a needed change — but sorting muddies the exact count.
Counting is cleaner: tally each half's letters and compare tallies directly instead of sorting.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting each half of size n/2 costs O(n log n). The comparison is O(n). Sorted copies use O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
The definition of anagram is 'same characters with the same multiplicities'. A natural first instinct is to sort each half so equal multisets line up, then measure how far apart they are.

**Why sorting feels right but is the long way around.** Sorting groups identical letters together, so two anagrams become byte-identical after sorting. To *count edits*, though, you don't actually care about order at all — you care about how many of each letter each half holds. Sorting throws away nothing useful but adds a log-factor and forces you to re-derive counts by scanning runs.

**Why we move on.** The whole computation is a histogram comparison. A histogram is built in one O(n) pass with a 26-slot array; sorting is strictly more work for the same information. Open with this to prove you know the anagram definition, then replace it with frequency counting.
approaches.insight: Sorting and frequency-counting both reduce a string to its multiset of characters. Counting reaches that multiset in O(n) with O(1) space, so prefer it the moment you only need per-letter totals.

dryRun.intro: Split, sort each half, then compare counts derived from the sorted runs.

java.explanation: Odd length can't split into equal halves — impossible.
Sorting is the baseline crutch; it isn't needed once we count letters.
Sum only the surplus of a over b — each surplus is one replacement.

python.explanation: Guard the odd-length impossible case first.
Sorting demonstrates the anagram idea but is unnecessary work.

python.line: return sum(max(0, count_a[c] - count_b[c]) for c in count_a)
python.explanation: Positive surpluses only — that's the change count.

diagrams.title: Halves as letter histograms
diagrams.caption: Each half collapses to a count vector; the answer is the positive gap.

pitfalls: Sorting then comparing positions instead of counts — fragile for measuring edits.
Forgetting the odd-length −1 guard before slicing.
Paying O(n log n) when an O(n) histogram gives the same answer.

edgeCases.behavior: Even length 0 → both halves empty → 0 changes.

approaches.name: Single Frequency-Difference Pass (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want — frame it as 'one histogram of (firstHalf − secondHalf), then sum the positives'.
hints: You don't need order — you need per-letter counts. What single array tracks the balance between the two halves?
Use one int[26]: increment for each char in the first half, decrement for each char in the second half.
After the pass, every positive entry is a letter the first half has in surplus. Sum those positives — that's the minimum number of replacements.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass over n characters with O(1) work each = O(n). A fixed 26-element array is O(1) extra space regardless of n.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a single `int[26]` balance array. Walk the first half adding `+1` to each letter's slot, then walk the second half subtracting `1`. After both passes, slot `c` holds `freq_a(c) − freq_b(c)`. The minimum number of changes is the sum of the *positive* slots.

**Why positive slots are exactly the edit count.** A positive value at letter `c` means the first half has that many more `c`s than the second half. To make the second half an anagram, each of those missing `c`s must be created by *replacing* some other character in the second half. Crucially, the surplus letters in `a` and the deficit letters in `b` come in matched pairs: every `+1` somewhere is balanced by a `−1` elsewhere, because both halves have the same length. So one replacement simultaneously removes a surplus and fills a deficit. Counting just the positives (or equivalently `sum(|balance|)/2`) avoids double-counting that single fix.

**Why O(1) space.** The alphabet is fixed at 26 letters, so the balance array never grows with `n`. That is the line to say aloud: 'O(n) time, O(1) space because the alphabet is constant.'

**Why the odd guard comes first.** If `n` is odd the halves differ in size and no number of replacements can equalise the multisets — return −1 before touching the array.
approaches.insight: Encoding 'first half minus second half' into one signed histogram turns a two-string comparison into a single sweep. The sum of positive surpluses equals `sum(|diff|)/2`; the /2 is the giveaway that one replacement heals both a surplus and a deficit at once — exactly what separates this from Making Anagrams.

dryRun.intro: n = 8, halves a = "xaxb", b = "bbxx". One signed histogram, then sum positives.

java.explanation: Odd length is impossible — short-circuit before any counting.

java.line: for (int i = 0; i < half; i++) balance[s.charAt(i) - 'a']++;
for (int i = half; i < n; i++) balance[s.charAt(i) - 'a']--;
java.explanation: Second half cancels with −1 per letter.
Each positive surplus is one forced replacement; deficits are already paid for.

python.explanation: Second half subtracts; zero means already balanced.

python.line: return sum(c for c in balance if c > 0)
python.explanation: Positive surplus total = minimum changes = sum(|diff|)/2.

diagrams.title: Signed balance histogram
diagrams.caption: First half adds, second subtracts; positives are the changes.

pitfalls: Summing |diff| without /2 — that overcounts because a surplus and its matching deficit are one fix.
Allocating a HashMap when a 26-int array is O(1) and faster.
Counting only one half and forgetting to subtract the other.

edgeCases.behavior: a="xy", b="yx" — identical multisets → balance all zero → 0 changes.
a="mn", b="op" — surplus m:+1, n:+1 → 2 changes.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the odd-length guard and slicing into unequal halves.
Summing absolute differences without dividing by two (that's Making Anagrams).
Using a HashMap with O(n) space when a 26-slot array is O(1).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Double-counting the difference
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Each replacement fixes a surplus in one half AND the matching deficit in the other at the same time. Summing all |diffs| counts both ends of that single fix.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: return sum(abs(count_a[c] - count_b[c]) for c in set(a) | set(b))
commonMistakesDetailed.good: return sum(max(0, count_a[c] - count_b[c]) for c in count_a)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the odd-length guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Slicing an odd string gives halves of size floor(n/2) and ceil(n/2); comparing them yields a wrong positive number instead of the required −1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
char[] a = s.substring(0, n / 2).toCharArray();
char[] b = s.substring(n / 2).toCharArray();

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Indexing the wrong second half
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Off-by-one on the split sends the middle character to the wrong half, corrupting both counts.

followupVariations.hint: Two separate strings, deletions allowed from both — answer is sum of ALL |diffs|, no /2.

followupVariations.title: Valid Anagram
followupVariations.hint: Just decide YES/NO — one frequency map, check it returns to all zeros.

followupVariations.hint: Bucket by the sorted (or count-tuple) signature of each word.

followupVariations.title: Find All Anagrams in a String
followupVariations.hint: Sliding window of fixed size with a running frequency match.

patternNote: Frequency-difference counting. Whenever a problem is about rearranging or replacing characters to reach an anagram, reduce each side to a 26-slot histogram and read the answer off the differences. Counting how many edits = sum of positive surpluses; counting deletions across both strings = sum of all absolute differences.
